claim: Circadian rhythms exist in Trichoderma atroviride.
source: Thus, we confirmed the existence of circadian rhythms in T. atroviride, which are temperature-compensated and modulated by environmental cues such as light and temperature.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that circadian rhythms were confirmed in T. atroviride, supported by experimental observations of TaFRQLUC oscillations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Circadian rhythms in T. atroviride are temperature-compensated.
source: Thus, we confirmed the existence of circadian rhythms in T. atroviride, which are temperature-compensated and modulated by environmental cues such as light and temperature.
evidence: Temperature compensation was demonstrated experimentally with Q10 calculation between 20-25°C yielding 1.05 ± 0.07, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Circadian rhythms in T. atroviride are modulated by environmental cues such as light and temperature.
source: Thus, we confirmed the existence of circadian rhythms in T. atroviride, which are temperature-compensated and modulated by environmental cues such as light and temperature.
evidence: Experimental data show that light pulses and temperature pulses can reset and entrain the clock, as demonstrated in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The presence of molecular rhythms in T. atroviride is highly dependent on the nutritional composition of the media.
source: Nevertheless, the presence of such molecular rhythms appears to be highly dependent on the nutritional composition of the media.
evidence: Experimental testing of multiple media showed oscillations only in GYEC media, which were improved with addition of peas, as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Complementation of a Neurospora crassa Δfrq strain with T. atroviride tafrq restored core clock function.
source: Complementation of a clock null (Δfrq) Neurospora crassa strain with the T. atroviride-negative clock component (tafrq) restored core clock function, with the same period observed in the latter fungus, confirming the role of tafrq as a bona fide core clock component.
evidence: Experimental complementation showed rhythmic luciferase expression with ~26 hr period in the complemented strain, as shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The period of circadian rhythms in the Δfrq::tafrq N. crassa strain is the same as observed in T. atroviride.
source: Complementation of a clock null (Δfrq) Neurospora crassa strain with the T. atroviride-negative clock component (tafrq) restored core clock function, with the same period observed in the latter fungus, confirming the role of tafrq as a bona fide core clock component.
evidence: Period measurements showed ~26 hr in both the TaFRQLUC reporter in T. atroviride and the Δfrq::tafrq N. crassa strain, as shown in Figures 1 and 2E.

claim: TaFRQ is a bona fide core clock component.
source: Complementation of a clock null (Δfrq) Neurospora crassa strain with the T. atroviride-negative clock component (tafrq) restored core clock function, with the same period observed in the latter fungus, confirming the role of tafrq as a bona fide core clock component.
evidence: Functional complementation in N. crassa and oscillations of TaFRQLUC in T. atroviride provide experimental evidence for TaFRQ as a core clock component.

claim: Light has an inhibitory effect on T. atroviride's mycoparasitic capabilities.
source: Confrontation assays between wild-type and clock mutant strains of T. atroviride and B. cinerea, in constant light or darkness, revealed an inhibitory effect of light on T. atroviride's mycoparasitic capabilities.
evidence: Confrontation assays showed higher overgrowth in DD compared to LL conditions, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: T. atroviride's overgrowth capacity is enhanced when inoculations are at dawn compared to dusk under light/dark cycles.
source: Interestingly, when confrontation assays were performed under light/dark cycles, T. atroviride's overgrowth capacity was enhanced when inoculations were at dawn compared to dusk.
evidence: Confrontation assays under LD cycles showed differential overgrowth depending on time of inoculation, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Deleting FRQ in B. cinerea is vital for the daily differential phenotype in mycoparasitic interactions.
source: Deleting the core clock-negative element FRQ in B. cinerea, but not in T. atroviride, was vital for the daily differential phenotype, suggesting that the B. cinerea clock has a more significant influence on the result of this interaction.
evidence: Confrontation assays with Δbcfrq1 showed loss of time-of-day differences, while Δtafrq maintained them, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: The B. cinerea clock has a more significant influence on the result of the T. atroviride-B. cinerea interaction than the T. atroviride clock.
source: Deleting the core clock-negative element FRQ in B. cinerea, but not in T. atroviride, was vital for the daily differential phenotype, suggesting that the B. cinerea clock has a more significant influence on the result of this interaction.
evidence: Differential effects of frq deletion in the two species on interaction outcomes, as shown in Figure 5, support this inference.

claim: T. atroviride clock components largely modulate development in this fungus.
source: Additionally, we observed that T. atroviride clock components largely modulate development and secondary metabolism in this fungus, including the rhythmic production of distinct volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
evidence: Conidiation assays showed altered developmental responses in clock mutants, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: T. atroviride clock components largely modulate secondary metabolism in this fungus.
source: Additionally, we observed that T. atroviride clock components largely modulate development and secondary metabolism in this fungus, including the rhythmic production of distinct volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
evidence: Metabolic fingerprinting showed altered production of diffusible compounds and VOCs in clock mutants, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: T. atroviride produces distinct volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in a rhythmic manner.
source: Additionally, we observed that T. atroviride clock components largely modulate development and secondary metabolism in this fungus, including the rhythmic production of distinct volatile organic compounds (VOCs).
evidence: Circadian metabolic profiling showed 17 VOCs with circadian rhythms in TaWT, as shown in Figure 6E and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Trichoderma species are cosmopolitan soil fungi found in several substrates.
source: Trichoderma species are cosmopolitan soil fungi found in several substrates, including decaying wood and fungal fruiting bodies, establishing beneficial interactions with plants (Carreras-Villaseñor et al., 2012; Kubicek et al., 2019; Vos et al., 2015), and negative ones with other microorganisms (Druzhinina et al., 2006; Guzman-Guzman et al., 2019; Harman et al., 2004; Sood et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species establish beneficial interactions with plants.
source: Trichoderma species are cosmopolitan soil fungi found in several substrates, including decaying wood and fungal fruiting bodies, establishing beneficial interactions with plants (Carreras-Villaseñor et al., 2012; Kubicek et al., 2019; Vos et al., 2015), and negative ones with other microorganisms (Druzhinina et al., 2006; Guzman-Guzman et al., 2019; Harman et al., 2004; Sood et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species establish negative interactions with other microorganisms.
source: Trichoderma species are cosmopolitan soil fungi found in several substrates, including decaying wood and fungal fruiting bodies, establishing beneficial interactions with plants (Carreras-Villaseñor et al., 2012; Kubicek et al., 2019; Vos et al., 2015), and negative ones with other microorganisms (Druzhinina et al., 2006; Guzman-Guzman et al., 2019; Harman et al., 2004; Sood et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species are well-known mycoparasites.
source: Trichoderma species are well-known mycoparasites as they can degrade, grow on other fungi, and even penetrate them, a distinctive feature that has been exploited in agriculture for their use as biocontrol agents of different phytopathogens, including Botrytis cinerea (Naglot et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species can degrade, grow on other fungi, and even penetrate them.
source: Trichoderma species are well-known mycoparasites as they can degrade, grow on other fungi, and even penetrate them, a distinctive feature that has been exploited in agriculture for their use as biocontrol agents of different phytopathogens, including Botrytis cinerea (Naglot et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species are used as biocontrol agents of different phytopathogens, including Botrytis cinerea.
source: Trichoderma species are well-known mycoparasites as they can degrade, grow on other fungi, and even penetrate them, a distinctive feature that has been exploited in agriculture for their use as biocontrol agents of different phytopathogens, including Botrytis cinerea (Naglot et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma's mycoparasitic behavior starts with the secretion of low levels of cell wall degrading enzymes (CWDE).
source: Trichoderma's mycoparasitic behavior starts with the secretion of low levels of cell wall degrading enzymes (CWDE) (Druzhinina et al., 2011; Seidl et al., 2009; Vos et al., 2015) that dismantle the fungal prey's hyphae.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cell wall degrading enzymes dismantle the fungal prey's hyphae.
source: Trichoderma's mycoparasitic behavior starts with the secretion of low levels of cell wall degrading enzymes (CWDE) (Druzhinina et al., 2011; Seidl et al., 2009; Vos et al., 2015) that dismantle the fungal prey's hyphae.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Small molecules derived from the host can function as molecular signals in Trichoderma, allowing prey recognition.
source: Release of small molecules derived from the host can function as molecular signals in Trichoderma, allowing prey recognition (Zeilinger et al., 2005), redirecting hyphal growth, and initiating coiling around the host mycelium, followed by hyphal penetration.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The synergistic effect of enhanced CWDE and toxic secondary metabolite production allows Trichoderma's hyphae to penetrate the prey's lumen, achieving its killing.
source: Indeed, the synergistic effect of enhanced CWDE and toxic secondary metabolite (SM) production allows Trichoderma's hyphae to penetrate the prey's lumen, achieving its killing (Belanger et al., 1995; Druzhinina et al., 2011; Sharma, 2011; Steyaert et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Conidiation induced by light has been extensively studied in Trichoderma species.
source: Trichoderma species present developmental responses to different stresses, of which conidiation induced by light and mechanical damage has been extensively studied (Casas-Flores and Herrera-Estrella, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Conidiation induced by mechanical damage has been extensively studied in Trichoderma species.
source: Trichoderma species present developmental responses to different stresses, of which conidiation induced by light and mechanical damage has been extensively studied (Casas-Flores and Herrera-Estrella, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Physical damage of mycelia in Trichoderma atroviride triggers a developmental injury response, leading to conidia production in the injured area through the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activation of MAPK signaling pathways.
source: Physical damage of mycelia in Trichoderma atroviride triggers a developmental injury response, leading to conidia production in the injured area through the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activation of MAPK signaling pathways (Hernández-Oñate et al., 2012; Medina-Castellanos et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Light is perceived as a stress signal in T. atroviride, triggering conidiation.
source: Additionally, light is also perceived as a stress signal, triggering conidiation: a light pulse (LP) given to a dark-grown T. atroviride generates several biochemical changes driving the formation of a green ring of conidia at the edge of the colony (Casas-Flores et al., 2004; Casas-Flores et al., 2006; Galun and Gressel, 1966; Schmoll et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A light pulse given to a dark-grown T. atroviride generates several biochemical changes driving the formation of a green ring of conidia at the edge of the colony.
source: Additionally, light is also perceived as a stress signal, triggering conidiation: a light pulse (LP) given to a dark-grown T. atroviride generates several biochemical changes driving the formation of a green ring of conidia at the edge of the colony (Casas-Flores et al., 2004; Casas-Flores et al., 2006; Galun and Gressel, 1966; Schmoll et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Two genes called blue light regulators 1 and 2 (blr1 and blr2) were identified as responsible for light-induced conidiation in T. atroviride.
source: In T. atroviride, two genes called blue light regulators 1 and 2 (blr1 and blr2) were identified as responsible for light-induced conidiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citation to Casas-Flores et al., 2004.

claim: The BLR proteins are homologs of the transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2.
source: The BLR proteins are homologs of the transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2, which in Neurospora crassa form the white collar complex (WCC), responsible for light and circadian regulation in this fungus (Casas-Flores et al., 2004; Froehlich et al., 2002; Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WC-1 and WC-2 form the white collar complex (WCC) in Neurospora crassa.
source: The BLR proteins are homologs of the transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2, which in Neurospora crassa form the white collar complex (WCC), responsible for light and circadian regulation in this fungus (Casas-Flores et al., 2004; Froehlich et al., 2002; Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The white collar complex (WCC) is responsible for light and circadian regulation in Neurospora crassa.
source: The BLR proteins are homologs of the transcription factors WC-1 and WC-2, which in Neurospora crassa form the white collar complex (WCC), responsible for light and circadian regulation in this fungus (Casas-Flores et al., 2004; Froehlich et al., 2002; Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Light can be directly perceived thanks to the presence of a light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) domain in WC-1/BLR1.
source: Importantly, light can be directly perceived thanks to the presence of a light-oxygen-voltage (LOV) domain in WC-1/BLR1 (Corrochano, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: BLRs are critical for the effect of light on growth in T. atroviride.
source: Furthermore, BLRs have been described as critical for the effect of light on growth, oxidative stress responses, and light-controlled gene expression (Cervantes-Badillo et al., 2013; Esquivel-Naranjo et al., 2016; Friedl et al., 2008a; Garcia-Esquivel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BLRs are critical for oxidative stress responses in T. atroviride.
source: Furthermore, BLRs have been described as critical for the effect of light on growth, oxidative stress responses, and light-controlled gene expression (Cervantes-Badillo et al., 2013; Esquivel-Naranjo et al., 2016; Friedl et al., 2008a; Garcia-Esquivel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BLRs are critical for light-controlled gene expression in T. atroviride.
source: Furthermore, BLRs have been described as critical for the effect of light on growth, oxidative stress responses, and light-controlled gene expression (Cervantes-Badillo et al., 2013; Esquivel-Naranjo et al., 2016; Friedl et al., 2008a; Garcia-Esquivel et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A frq homolog is present in T. atroviride that is induced by light.
source: Studies on BLR1 and BLR2 and the presence of a frq homolog that is induced by light, and whose expression depends on BLR1 (Garcia-Esquivel et al., 2016; Steyaert et al., 2010a), suggest the presence of a functional clock and underlying circadian regulation in this fungus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The expression of the frq homolog in T. atroviride depends on BLR1.
source: Studies on BLR1 and BLR2 and the presence of a frq homolog that is induced by light, and whose expression depends on BLR1 (Garcia-Esquivel et al., 2016; Steyaert et al., 2010a), suggest the presence of a functional clock and underlying circadian regulation in this fungus.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neither circadian oscillations of tafrq/TaFRQ levels nor circadian phenotypes have been reported in T. atroviride to date.
source: However, to date, neither circadian oscillations of tafrq/TaFRQ levels nor circadian phenotypes have been reported in T. atroviride; meanwhile, various studies have failed at detecting overt or molecular circadian rhythms in several fungi across fungal clades (Cascant-Lopez et al., 2020; Hevia et al., 2016; Larrondo and Canessa, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature indicating lack of prior reports.

claim: Various studies have failed at detecting overt or molecular circadian rhythms in several fungi across fungal clades.
source: However, to date, neither circadian oscillations of tafrq/TaFRQ levels nor circadian phenotypes have been reported in T. atroviride; meanwhile, various studies have failed at detecting overt or molecular circadian rhythms in several fungi across fungal clades (Cascant-Lopez et al., 2020; Hevia et al., 2016; Larrondo and Canessa, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Circadian rhythms have emerged as an adaptation to Earth's rotation around its axis.
source: Circadian rhythms have emerged as an adaptation to Earth's rotation around its axis, allowing organisms to keep track of time, anticipating and adapting to periodic and predictable environmental changes through the temporal coordination of gene expression, metabolic pathways, physiological responses, and even behaviors (Bell-Pedersen et al., 2005; Hurley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Interactions between organisms may be subjected to circadian regulation.
source: Recent findings have shown that interactions between organisms may also be subjected to circadian regulation (reviewed in Hevia et al., 2016; Larrondo and Canessa, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The interaction between the phytopathogenic fungus B. cinerea and Arabidopsis thaliana largely depends on the fungal functional circadian clock.
source: Yet, it has been reported that the interaction between the phytopathogenic fungus B. cinerea and Arabidopsis thaliana largely depends on the fungal functional circadian clock, with virulence reaching higher levels at nighttime (Hevia et al., 2015; Ingle et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B. cinerea virulence reaches higher levels at nighttime.
source: Yet, it has been reported that the interaction between the phytopathogenic fungus B. cinerea and Arabidopsis thaliana largely depends on the fungal functional circadian clock, with virulence reaching higher levels at nighttime (Hevia et al., 2015; Ingle et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: N. crassa is a salient model in chronobiology due to its robust circadian phenotype of daily spore production at dawn and a wealth of molecular resources.
source: The ascomycete N. crassa is a salient model in chronobiology due to its robust circadian phenotype of daily spore production at dawn and a wealth of molecular resources (Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The N. crassa central oscillator is based on a negative transcriptional–translational feedback loop (TTFL).
source: Its central oscillator is based on a negative transcriptional–translational feedback loop (TTFL), a shared core architecture across phyla (Dunlap, 1999; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Loros, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The TTFL is a shared core architecture across phyla.
source: Its central oscillator is based on a negative transcriptional–translational feedback loop (TTFL), a shared core architecture across phyla (Dunlap, 1999; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Loros, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In N. crassa, the WCC activates the expression of frequency (frq).
source: In N. crassa, the WCC activates the expression of the TTFL-negative element, frequency (frq), which leads to increasing levels of the FRQ protein, that starts recruiting kinases and negatively regulates its own expression by phosphorylating and inactivating the WCC.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge of the N. crassa circadian system.

claim: FRQ negatively regulates its own expression by phosphorylating and inactivating the WCC in N. crassa.
source: In N. crassa, the WCC activates the expression of the TTFL-negative element, frequency (frq), which leads to increasing levels of the FRQ protein, that starts recruiting kinases and negatively regulates its own expression by phosphorylating and inactivating the WCC.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge of the N. crassa circadian system.

claim: Both frq mRNA and FRQ protein levels oscillate with a period close to 22.5 hr in N. crassa.
source: Both frq mRNA and FRQ protein levels oscillate during this process with a period close to 22.5 hr (Larrondo et al., 2015; Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: wc-1, wc-2, and frq homologs are present in several fungi.
source: Albeit wc-1, wc-2, and frq homologs are present in several fungi, the description of overt clock phenotypes, as the molecular characterization of circadian rhythms in fungal species besides N. crassa, has been limited (Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015; Salichos and Rokas, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The description of overt clock phenotypes in fungal species besides N. crassa has been limited.
source: Albeit wc-1, wc-2, and frq homologs are present in several fungi, the description of overt clock phenotypes, as the molecular characterization of circadian rhythms in fungal species besides N. crassa, has been limited (Montenegro-Montero et al., 2015; Salichos and Rokas, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Rhythms in BcFRQ1 levels were confirmed in B. cinerea.
source: Among these is B. cinerea, where rhythms in BcFRQ1 levels were confirmed, along with BcFRQ1's key role in conferring the daily difference on virulence potential.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citation to Hevia et al., 2015.

claim: BcFRQ1 plays a key role in conferring the daily difference on virulence potential in B. cinerea.
source: Among these is B. cinerea, where rhythms in BcFRQ1 levels were confirmed, along with BcFRQ1's key role in conferring the daily difference on virulence potential.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citation to Hevia et al., 2015.

claim: In B. cinerea, BcFRQ1 plays an extra-circadian role in developmental decisions.
source: Remarkably, the evidence also suggests that in B. cinerea BcFRQ1 plays an extra-circadian role in developmental decisions as Δbcfrq1 displays altered developmental phenotypes observed even under conditions where the clock function is abolished, such as constant light, and in contrast to the phenotype observed in the absence of BcWCL1 (Hevia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Δbcfrq1 displays altered developmental phenotypes observed even under conditions where the clock function is abolished, such as constant light.
source: Remarkably, the evidence also suggests that in B. cinerea BcFRQ1 plays an extra-circadian role in developmental decisions as Δbcfrq1 displays altered developmental phenotypes observed even under conditions where the clock function is abolished, such as constant light, and in contrast to the phenotype observed in the absence of BcWCL1 (Hevia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TaFRQLUC oscillations have an average period of 26.5 ± 0.36 hr.
source: The period estimation of those oscillations by fast Fourier transform nonlinear least squares (FFT-NLS) using BioDare (Zielinski et al., 2014) revealed an average period of 26.5 ± 0.36 hr.
evidence: Period was calculated from experimental data using BioDare analysis.

claim: The phase of the first peak of TaFRQ expression occurs at DD 22, which corresponds to circadian time CT8.
source: The phase of the first peak of TaFRQ expression occurs at DD 22, which corresponds to circadian time CT8, and is roughly similar (albeit slightly advanced) compared to the phase of FRQLUC expression (CT11) described in N. crassa (Larrondo et al., 2012).
evidence: Phase was determined from experimental data and compared to published N. crassa data.

claim: The Q10 for TaFRQLUC oscillations between 20 and 25°C is 1.05 ± 0.07.
source: To quantify the degree of temperature compensation, we calculated the Q10 between 20 and 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), obtaining a Q10 of 1.05 ± 0.07, which is in the range for temperature compensation described in other circadian systems (Anderson et al., 1985; Kusakina et al., 2014; Mattern et al., 1982).
evidence: Q10 was calculated from experimental period measurements at different temperatures.

claim: The Q10 of 1.05 ± 0.07 is in the range for temperature compensation described in other circadian systems.
source: To quantify the degree of temperature compensation, we calculated the Q10 between 20 and 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), obtaining a Q10 of 1.05 ± 0.07, which is in the range for temperature compensation described in other circadian systems (Anderson et al., 1985; Kusakina et al., 2014; Mattern et al., 1982).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to published literature on temperature compensation.

claim: The Ncc-box-luc reporter reveals clear rhythms of luc levels under free-running conditions (DD) in T. atroviride.
source: Notably, this reporter revealed clear rhythms of luc levels under free-running conditions (DD), which responded to light and temperature cues, and whose presence was also conditioned by culture media composition (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data show rhythmic bioluminescence in the Ncc-box-luc reporter strain.

claim: The Ncc-box-luc reporter rhythms respond to light and temperature cues in T. atroviride.
source: Notably, this reporter revealed clear rhythms of luc levels under free-running conditions (DD), which responded to light and temperature cues, and whose presence was also conditioned by culture media composition (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data show response to light pulses and temperature pulses, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Ncc-box-luc reporter has an average period of 25.67 ± 1.01 hr in T. atroviride.
source: The bioluminescent traces were analyzed using BioDare (Zielinski et al., 2014), revealing an average of 25.67 ± 1.01 hr period for two independent Ncc-box-luc strains, in close agreement with the TaFRQLUC data.
evidence: Period was calculated from experimental data using BioDare analysis.

claim: A pivotal Neurospora cis-element (Ncc-box) can be recognized in T. atroviride.
source: This provides additional proof of a functional circadian clock in T. atroviride and demonstrates that a pivotal Neurospora cis-element (Ncc-box) can be recognized in T. atroviride.
evidence: The functional activity of the Ncc-box-luc reporter in T. atroviride demonstrates recognition of this cis-element.

claim: 82.6% (19/23) of phosphorylation sites characterized in N. crassa FRQ are preserved in TaFRQ.
source: In TaFRQ, 82.6% (19/23) of such sites are preserved, with the divergent ones all residing in the C-terminal portion of the protein, after the PEST-2 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 demonstrates conservation of phosphorylation sites.

claim: The divergent phosphorylation sites between N. crassa FRQ and TaFRQ all reside in the C-terminal portion of the protein, after the PEST-2 domain.
source: In TaFRQ, 82.6% (19/23) of such sites are preserved, with the divergent ones all residing in the C-terminal portion of the protein, after the PEST-2 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 demonstrates location of divergent sites.

claim: Δtafrq exhibited a dark-green color at 72 hr post-inoculation in LL, not observed in TaWT or OE::tafrq strains.
source: In contrast, the Δtafrq strain exhibited a dark-green color not observed also in the OE::tafrq strains (Figure 3A).
evidence: Visual observation documented in Figure 3A shows the phenotypic difference.

claim: At 3 days post-inoculation, Δtafrq had produced fewer conidia than TaWT.
source: Notably, at 3 days post-inoculation (dpi), Δtafrq had produced fewer conidia, albeit this difference was no longer significant by day 7, indicating that conidiation in Δtafrq is delayed but not fully compromised.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3B demonstrate reduced conidiation at 3 dpi.

claim: Conidiation in Δtafrq is delayed but not fully compromised.
source: Notably, at 3 days post-inoculation (dpi), Δtafrq had produced fewer conidia, albeit this difference was no longer significant by day 7, indicating that conidiation in Δtafrq is delayed but not fully compromised.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3B demonstrate recovery of conidiation by day 7.

claim: Conidia formation in response to a discrete LP was significantly decreased in Δtafrq, regardless of the pulse duration.
source: Furthermore, conidia formation in response to a discrete LP was significantly decreased in Δtafrq, regardless of the pulse duration (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3C demonstrate reduced conidiation after light pulses.

claim: No significant differences in conidiation were observed between TaWT and OE::tafrq in LL or after light pulses.
source: In contrast, no significant differences were observed between TaWT and OE::tafrq in both types of analyses (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3B and C demonstrate no significant differences.

claim: Δblr1 showed a 51% average reduction in conidia production compared to the TaWT strain after mechanical injury.
source: Interestingly, Δblr1 showed a 51% average reduction in conidia production compared to the TaWT strain, which had not been previously reported.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3D demonstrate reduced conidiation in Δblr1.

claim: Δtafrq exhibited almost a 100-fold reduction in injure-triggered conidiation.
source: In contrast, while the OE::tafrq showed no significant differences compared to TaWT, Δtafrq exhibited almost a 100-fold reduction in injure-triggered conidiation (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3D demonstrate dramatic reduction in conidiation after injury.

claim: Complementing Δtafrq with tafrq back at its endogenous locus restored the injury-response conidiation.
source: As expected, we were able to restore the injury-response conidiation when complementing Δtafrq with tafrq back at its endogenous locus (ΔtafrqC) (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 demonstrate restoration of conidiation in complemented strains.

claim: In the TaWT–B05.10 interaction, T. atroviride displayed higher overgrowth over B. cinerea in DD than in LL (50% vs. 20%, respectively).
source: In the TaWT–B05.10 interaction, T. atroviride displayed higher overgrowth over B. cinerea in DD than in LL (50% vs. 20%, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate differential overgrowth in different light conditions.

claim: Δblr1 displayed increased overgrowth in DD (90%) versus LL against B05.10.
source: Increased overgrowth in DD (90%) versus LL was also seen for Δblr1 against B05.10, being the most aggressive of the tested T. atroviride strains.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate high overgrowth by Δblr1 in DD.

claim: Δblr1 is the most aggressive of the tested T. atroviride strains against B05.10.
source: Increased overgrowth in DD (90%) versus LL was also seen for Δblr1 against B05.10, being the most aggressive of the tested T. atroviride strains.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate highest overgrowth by Δblr1.

claim: Δtafrq displayed similar behavior to TaWT in LL and DD against B05.10.
source: At the same time, Δtafrq displayed similar behavior to TaWT in LL and DD against B05.10 (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate similar overgrowth patterns.

claim: Under LL, Botrytis Δbcwcl1 was easily overgrown by TaWT but not by the Δblr1 or Δtafrq Trichoderma mutants.
source: Finally, under LL, Botrytis Δbcwcl1 was easily overgrown by TaWT but not by the Δblr1 or Δtafrq Trichoderma mutants.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate differential overgrowth patterns.

claim: In the absence of light, Δbcwcl1 was easily overgrown by ~80% by all Trichoderma strains.
source: However, in the absence of light, Δbcwcl1 was easily overgrown by ~80% by all Trichoderma strains (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 4C demonstrate high overgrowth in DD.

claim: In TaWT–B05.10 interactions under LD cycles, Trichoderma's overgrowth was enhanced in plates inoculated at dawn (AM) rather than at dusk (PM).
source: In TaWT–B05.10 interactions under LD cycles, Trichoderma's overgrowth was enhanced in plates inoculated at dawn (AM) rather than at dusk (PM) (Figure 5B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 5C demonstrate differential overgrowth based on time of inoculation.

claim: The Δtafrq–B05.10 interactions behaved similarly to TaWT-B05.10 under LD cycles.
source: The Δtafrq–B05.10 interactions behaved similarly to TaWT-B05.10, suggesting that TaFRQ does not cause the differential mycoparasitic behavior seen in LD (enhanced capacity under the AM inoculation protocol).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 5C demonstrate similar patterns for Δtafrq and TaWT.

claim: TaFRQ does not cause the differential mycoparasitic behavior seen in LD cycles.
source: The Δtafrq–B05.10 interactions behaved similarly to TaWT-B05.10, suggesting that TaFRQ does not cause the differential mycoparasitic behavior seen in LD (enhanced capacity under the AM inoculation protocol).
evidence: The similar behavior of Δtafrq and TaWT suggests TaFRQ is not responsible for the time-of-day effect.

claim: Δblr1 was capable of overgrowing WT Botrytis to the same extent in both AM and PM inoculation protocols.
source: In contrast, Δblr1 was capable of overgrowing WT Botrytis to the same extent in both AM and PM inoculation protocols, suggesting that indeed, BRL1 has a role in the differential outcome of interactions performed in LD cycles (Figure 5B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 5C demonstrate no time-of-day difference for Δblr1.

claim: BLR1 has a role in the differential outcome of interactions performed in LD cycles.
source: In contrast, Δblr1 was capable of overgrowing WT Botrytis to the same extent in both AM and PM inoculation protocols, suggesting that indeed, BRL1 has a role in the differential outcome of interactions performed in LD cycles (Figure 5B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The loss of time-of-day difference in Δblr1 suggests BLR1 is involved in this phenomenon.

claim: Δbcfrq1 was overgrown by all Trichoderma strains to the same extent in both AM and PM cycles.
source: Centering the analysis on B. cinerea, Δbcfrq1 was overgrown by all Trichoderma strains to the same extent in both cycles (AM or PM), revealing the disappearance of the clock-related phenotypes observed for B05.10.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 5C demonstrate no time-of-day difference with Δbcfrq1.

claim: The absence of BcFRQ1 causes disappearance of the clock-related phenotypes observed for B05.10.
source: Centering the analysis on B. cinerea, Δbcfrq1 was overgrown by all Trichoderma strains to the same extent in both cycles (AM or PM), revealing the disappearance of the clock-related phenotypes observed for B05.10.
evidence: The loss of time-of-day difference in interactions with Δbcfrq1 demonstrates the role of BcFRQ1.

claim: The production of 230 diffusible compounds was statistically different among strains and conditions.
source: The production of 230 compounds was statistically different among strains and conditions (ANOVA p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data identified 230 differentially produced compounds.

claim: Production of diffusible compounds is particularly enhanced in Δtafrq in all conditions compared to TaWT, Δblr1, and OE::tafrq.
source: The overview of diffusible compounds produced by TaWT, Δblr1, Δtafrq, and OE::tafrq in DD, LL, and LP (Figure 6A) indicates that production of diffusible compounds is particularly enhanced in Δtafrq in all conditions compared to TaWT, Δblr1, and OE::tafrq.
evidence: Heatmap analysis shown in Figure 6A demonstrates enhanced compound production in Δtafrq.

claim: In TaWT, 103 molecules showed a twofold induction in LL compared to DD.
source: In TaWT, 103 and 15 molecules showed a twofold induction in LL and LP compared to DD, respectively, which suggests that light induces the production of diffusible compounds in T. atroviride.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mass spectrometry data identified light-induced compounds.

claim: Light induces the production of diffusible compounds in T. atroviride.
source: In TaWT, 103 and 15 molecules showed a twofold induction in LL and LP compared to DD, respectively, which suggests that light induces the production of diffusible compounds in T. atroviride.
evidence: The observation of light-induced compounds supports this inference.

claim: 129 molecules were at least twofold reduced in LL in Δblr1 compared to TaWT.
source: A comparison of diffusible compound levels between TaWT and Δblr1 showed that 129 molecules were at least twofold reduced in LL in the mutant strain.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mass spectrometry data identified reduced compounds in Δblr1.

claim: BLR1 is necessary for light induction of several diffusible compounds in TaWT.
source: This suggests that BLR1 is necessary for light induction of several diffusible compounds in TaWT, including 1679.08 m/z, as their production is severely dampened in the Δblr1 mutant in LL.
evidence: The reduction of light-induced compounds in Δblr1 supports this inference.

claim: TaFRQ represses the production of diffusible compounds under the tested conditions.
source: This suggests that TaFRQ represses the production of diffusible compounds under these conditions.
evidence: The enhanced production of compounds in Δtafrq supports this inference.

claim: The production of 131 volatile organic compounds was statistically different across all strains and growth conditions.
source: The analyses revealed that the production of 131 compounds (in a 50–500 m/z range) was statistically different across all strains and growth conditions (ANOVA p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of LTP-MS data identified 131 differentially produced VOCs.

claim: Production of VOCs is enhanced in LL in Δblr1 and Δtafrq.
source: A global view of VOCs reveals an enhanced production in LL in Δblr1 and Δtafrq, with a group of VOCs mainly induced in Δblr1 and reduced in Δtafrq.
evidence: Heatmap analysis shown in Figure 6C demonstrates enhanced VOC production.

claim: 6-pentyl-α-pyrone (6-PP) is induced in DD compared to LL in TaWT.
source: In TaWT, few VOCs depicted differences between light conditions, being one of them the well-known antifungal volatile compound 6-pentyl-α-pyrone (6-PP) (167.07 m/z). This compound showed to be induced in DD compared to LL, suggesting an inhibitory effect of light in 6-PP production (Figure 6D).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6D demonstrate higher 6-PP levels in DD.

claim: Light has an inhibitory effect on 6-PP production in TaWT.
source: In TaWT, few VOCs depicted differences between light conditions, being one of them the well-known antifungal volatile compound 6-pentyl-α-pyrone (6-PP) (167.07 m/z). This compound showed to be induced in DD compared to LL, suggesting an inhibitory effect of light in 6-PP production (Figure 6D).
evidence: The higher levels of 6-PP in DD compared to LL support this inference.

claim: In Δblr1, 6-PP production showed a 5.8-fold induction in LL compared to TaWT.
source: In Δblr1, 6-PP production showed a 5.8-fold induction in LL, but no significant differences were observed in DD and LP compared to TaWT.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6D demonstrate increased 6-PP in Δblr1 under LL.

claim: A dramatic reduction of 6-PP production was observed in Δtafrq in DD, LL, and LP.
source: Interestingly, a dramatic reduction of 6-PP production was observed in Δtafrq in DD, LL, and LP (61, 10, and 3 negative fold change, respectively) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6D demonstrate reduced 6-PP in Δtafrq.

claim: 17 volatile compounds exhibited a circadian profile with a calculated period between 24 and 26 hr in TaWT.
source: Rhythmicity of VOC levels was calculated using BioDare (with FFT-NLS and BD2eLTK cycle algorithms with a p-value<0.05), observing that 17 compounds exhibited a circadian profile with a calculated period between 24 and 26 hr in TaWT (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Circadian analysis of VOC data identified 17 rhythmic compounds, as detailed in Supplementary file 4.

claim: In Δtafrq, most rhythmic VOC compounds (13 out of 17) lost rhythmicity.
source: In Δtafrq, as expected, most compounds profiles (13 out of the 17) lost rhythmicity (see Supplementary file 4) and, importantly, the remaining four compounds (63.83 m/z, 90.83 m/z, 388.87 m/z, and 389.77 m/z) exhibited weak oscillatory behavior (e.g., reduced amplitude and altered phase) as determined after manual examination of compounds dynamics (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Analysis of VOC rhythmicity in Δtafrq showed loss of rhythms for most compounds.

claim: The production of some VOCs in T. atroviride is under circadian control.
source: In total, these results suggest that the production of some VOCs in T. atroviride is under circadian control.
evidence: The observation of rhythmic VOCs in TaWT that lose rhythmicity in Δtafrq supports this inference.

claim: T. atroviride IMI 206040 was initially isolated from a plum tree of the Czar variety in an orchard in Urshult near Växjö in southern Sweden.
source: T. atroviride IMI 206040, initially isolated from a plum tree of the Czar variety in an orchard in Urshult near Växjö in southern Sweden (EFSA European Food Safety, 2015), was used as wild-type strain (TaWT) and, along with Δblr1, described by Casas-Flores et al., 2004, were kindly provided by Dr. Alfredo Herrera-Estrella.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published source.

claim: B. cinerea B05.10 was initially isolated from Vitis vinifera (Germany).
source: B. cinerea B05.10 Pers. Fr. [Botryotinia fuckeliana (de Bary) Whetzel] was initially isolated from Vitis vinifera (Germany) and was provided by the Tudzinsky laboratory (WWU, Germany).
evidence: This statement provides the origin of the strain used in the study.

claim: The DNA binding domains of WC-1 and BLR1 share a 97.2% aa identity.
source: As the DNA binding domains of WC-1 and BLR1 share a 97.2% aa identity, we hypothesize that the BRL1/BLR2 complex can recognize the Ncc-box element driving circadian oscillations and that a similar c-box sequence could be found in the tafrq promoter.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citation to Casas-Flores et al., 2004.

claim: The BRL1/BLR2 complex can recognize the Ncc-box element driving circadian oscillations.
source: As the DNA binding domains of WC-1 and BLR1 share a 97.2% aa identity, we hypothesize that the BRL1/BLR2 complex can recognize the Ncc-box element driving circadian oscillations and that a similar c-box sequence could be found in the tafrq promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the high sequence identity and the functional activity of the Ncc-box reporter.

claim: A similar c-box sequence could be found in the tafrq promoter.
source: As the DNA binding domains of WC-1 and BLR1 share a 97.2% aa identity, we hypothesize that the BRL1/BLR2 complex can recognize the Ncc-box element driving circadian oscillations and that a similar c-box sequence could be found in the tafrq promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the recognition of the Ncc-box and the expected mechanism of circadian regulation.

claim: Two putative light response elements in the tafrq's promoter with a putative GATA box consensus sequence exist at proximal and distal locations.
source: Two putative light response elements in the tafrq's promoter with a putative GATA box consensus sequence at proximal and distal locations (−355 to –319 and –1180 to –1171 from the TSS, respectively) have been postulated (Cervantes-Badillo et al., 2013), of which one of them could be acting as a putative Tacbox sequence.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Comparison of the tafrq and ncfrq sequences shows 54% identity at the DNA level.
source: Comparison of the tafrq and ncfrq sequences informs a 54 and 50% of identity at the DNA and protein levels, respectively (using Clustal Omega multiple sequence alignment), which provides sufficient functional conservation to allow rescuing of the core clock function in a N. crassa arrhythmic strain.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis provides this quantitative measure.

claim: Comparison of the tafrq and ncfrq sequences shows 50% identity at the protein level.
source: Comparison of the tafrq and ncfrq sequences informs a 54 and 50% of identity at the DNA and protein levels, respectively (using Clustal Omega multiple sequence alignment), which provides sufficient functional conservation to allow rescuing of the core clock function in a N. crassa arrhythmic strain.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis provides this quantitative measure.

claim: The sequence identity between tafrq and ncfrq provides sufficient functional conservation to allow rescuing of the core clock function in a N. crassa arrhythmic strain.
source: Comparison of the tafrq and ncfrq sequences informs a 54 and 50% of identity at the DNA and protein levels, respectively (using Clustal Omega multiple sequence alignment), which provides sufficient functional conservation to allow rescuing of the core clock function in a N. crassa arrhythmic strain.
evidence: The successful complementation experiment demonstrates this functional conservation.

claim: TaFRQ is acting as a negative element in Neurospora.
source: Thus, in addition to the complementation itself, it is the fact that TaFRQ is indeed acting as a negative element in Neurospora, which can be clearly inferred by the overall decrease of WCC activity (as seen by the reduction in luciferase expression when compared to the recipient strain).
evidence: The reduction in luciferase expression in the complemented strain compared to the Δfrq strain demonstrates negative regulation.

claim: Period determinants are encoded in the TaFRQ protein sequence.
source: Importantly, as we restored the core clock in Δfrq, the resulting oscillations reflected the endogenous ~26 hr period originally observed in T. atroviride, instead of the Neurospora WT rhythm of ~22 hr, implying that period determinants are encoded in the TaFRQ protein sequence and that they are 'read' by the rest of the circadian machinery in a proper manner, despite the phylogenetic distance of both genera.
evidence: The observation that the complemented strain exhibits the T. atroviride period rather than the N. crassa period demonstrates that period is encoded in TaFRQ.

claim: The quality of FRQ regarding phosphorylation status rather than its stability or half-life is important for period length.
source: Recent studies have shown that the quality of FRQ regarding phosphorylation status rather than its stability or half-life is important for period length (Larrondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The impact of nutrient availability on certain aspects of circadian rhythms has been observed from mammals to N. crassa.
source: While the impact of nutrient availability in certain aspects of circadian rhythms has been observed from mammals to N. crassa (Bae et al., 2019; Oosterman et al., 2015), our results indicate an even bigger dependence on culture conditions in allowing molecular visualization of the Trichoderma clock.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The use of different carbon sources in culture media allows observation of photostimulation of growth and conidiation in the dark in T. atroviride.
source: In T. atroviride, the use of different carbon sources in culture media allows, in some cases, observation of photostimulation of growth and conidiation in the dark, processes in which BLR1 plays a critical role in carbon-source selectivity (Friedl et al., 2008a; Friedl et al., 2008b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: C:N ratios are relevant environmental factors influencing conidiation in Trichoderma.
source: Also, C:N ratios are relevant environmental factors influencing conidiation in Trichoderma (Steyaert et al., 2010b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Organic nitrogen sources in culture media have been described as important for fungal mycoparasitic behavior.
source: Additionally, organic nitrogen sources in culture media have been described as important for fungal mycoparasitic behavior (Barnett, 1963).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Nitrogen sources are known to affect growth in Trichoderma species.
source: Also, nitrogen sources are known to affect growth in Trichoderma species (Danielson and Davey, 1973; Nolan and Nolan, 1972).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The plant circadian clock could alter the composition and function of the rhizosphere microbiome.
source: Indeed, the plant circadian clock could alter the composition and function of the rhizosphere microbiome as it has been observed in the rhizosphere of WT and long/short period mutants of A. thaliana (Hubbard et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Rhythmically structured metabolic exchanges between organisms in the community in collective benefit could be occurring.
source: Rhythmically structured metabolic exchanges between the organisms in the community in collective benefit could be occurring (Sartor et al., 2019), although it still remains to be studied in this context.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: In fungi, little is known about FRQ function besides N. crassa and B. cinerea.
source: In fungi, little is known about FRQ function besides N. crassa and B. cinerea.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A recent study of frq in V. dahliae found no significant phenotypic differences in the deletion strain regarding sporulation and microsclerotia formation in DD or LD.
source: A recent study of frq in the phytopathogen V. dahliae found no significant phenotypic differences in the deletion strain regarding sporulation and microsclerotia formation in DD or LD (Cascant-Lopez et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In M. robertsii, FRQ is necessary for ring formation under LD 12:12.
source: Similarly, in the entomopathogenic fungi Metarhizium robertsii, FRQ is necessary for ring formation under LD 12:12, although neither the WT nor the mutant strain displayed such rings under DD conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent citation to Peng et al., 2022.

claim: M. robertsii FRQ is dispensable in almost all evaluated phenotypes including virulence against Galleria mellonella.
source: Besides this, M. robertsii FRQ is dispensable in almost all evaluated phenotypes (growth and conidiation in different stress conditions), including virulence against Galleria mellonella (Peng et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Studies in B. bassiana and M. oryzae have shown that their frq knockouts exhibit diminished conidiation and virulence.
source: Meanwhile, studies in Beauveria bassiana (in which two frq homologs exists) and M. oryzae strain Guy11 have shown that their frq knockouts exhibit diminished conidiation and virulence against G. mellonella (Tong et al., 2021) and rice seedlings (Shi et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SMs have been related to developmental programs in fungi.
source: SMs have been related to developmental programs in fungi and could have a role in response to damage in T. atroviride (Atriztán-Hernández et al., 2019; Schmoll et al., 2010; Tisch and Schmoll, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: After injury and fungivory, a group of VOCs, including 6-PP, increase in TaWT but not in the MAPK mutant Δtmk3.
source: Reports show that after injury and fungivory a group of VOCs, including 6-PP, increase in TaWT but not in the MAPK mutant Δtmk3 (Atriztán-Hernández et al., 2019), which shows diminished conidiation after an injury as observed in the Δtafrq mutant (Medina-Castellanos et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Δtmk3 shows diminished conidiation after an injury.
source: Reports show that after injury and fungivory a group of VOCs, including 6-PP, increase in TaWT but not in the MAPK mutant Δtmk3 (Atriztán-Hernández et al., 2019), which shows diminished conidiation after an injury as observed in the Δtafrq mutant (Medina-Castellanos et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Oxylipin could be involved in signaling after damage in T. atroviride.
source: Additionally, it was previously suggested that oxylipin could be involved in signaling after damage (Medina-Castellanos et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The reduction of injury-induced conidiation in Δtafrq could be related to its dysregulated diffusible and VOC production profiles.
source: We propose that the reduction of injury-induced conidiation in Δtafrq could be related to its dysregulated diffusible and VOC production profiles, in which further studies identifying those compounds could shed light on their role in injury-induced conidiation.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the observed correlations between metabolite profiles and conidiation phenotypes.

claim: A light-repression effect on 6-PP production was observed in T. atroviride P1 and IMI 206040 strains when grown under LD and DD conditions.
source: A light-repression effect on 6-PP production was also observed in T. atroviride P1 and IMI 206040 strains when 6-PP production was analyzed under LD and DD conditions (Speckbacher et al., 2020a; Contreras-Cornejo et al., 2022) and when grown in different light wavelengths (Moreno-Ruiz et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Light regulation of SMs has been reported in several fungi.
source: Light regulation of SMs has been reported in several fungi (Tisch and Schmoll, 2010) as the involvement of WC-1 homologs in Cercospora zeae-maydis and Fusarium graminearum as repressors of cercosporin and trichothecene production, respectively (Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WC-1 homologs act as repressors of cercosporin production in Cercospora zeae-maydis.
source: Light regulation of SMs has been reported in several fungi (Tisch and Schmoll, 2010) as the involvement of WC-1 homologs in Cercospora zeae-maydis and Fusarium graminearum as repressors of cercosporin and trichothecene production, respectively (Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WC-1 homologs act as repressors of trichothecene production in Fusarium graminearum.
source: Light regulation of SMs has been reported in several fungi (Tisch and Schmoll, 2010) as the involvement of WC-1 homologs in Cercospora zeae-maydis and Fusarium graminearum as repressors of cercosporin and trichothecene production, respectively (Kim et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The involvement of TaFRQ in the production of SMs in T. atroviride has not been reported to date.
source: Nevertheless, the involvement of TaFRQ in the production of SMs in T. atroviride (or FRQ of any other fungus) has not been reported to date.
evidence: This statement reflects the novelty of the current findings.

claim: How daily rhythms impact metabolite levels in Neurospora has not been described so far.
source: On the contrary, in Neurospora how these daily rhythms impact metabolite levels has not been described so far, despite ample efforts that have systematically shown the clock's influence on its transcriptome and proteome (Hurley et al., 2014; Hurley et al., 2018; Sancar et al., 2015), suggesting temporal compartmentalization of metabolism at large, with catabolic and anabolic reactions concentrated at dawn and dusk, respectively (Hurley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature showing transcriptome and proteome studies but not metabolite studies.

claim: The clock's influence on the transcriptome and proteome in Neurospora suggests temporal compartmentalization of metabolism at large, with catabolic and anabolic reactions concentrated at dawn and dusk, respectively.
source: On the contrary, in Neurospora how these daily rhythms impact metabolite levels has not been described so far, despite ample efforts that have systematically shown the clock's influence on its transcriptome and proteome (Hurley et al., 2014; Hurley et al., 2018; Sancar et al., 2015), suggesting temporal compartmentalization of metabolism at large, with catabolic and anabolic reactions concentrated at dawn and dusk, respectively (Hurley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Trichoderma species' antagonistic capacity is correlated with their ability to produce 6-PP.
source: Trichoderma species' antagonistic capacity is correlated with their ability to produce 6-PP (Reino et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Similar inhibitory effects of light in mycoparasitism in T. atroviride have been reported against Fusarium oxysporum.
source: Similar inhibitory effects of light in mycoparasitism in T. atroviride have been reported against Fusarium oxysporum (Moreno-Ruiz et al., 2020; Speckbacher et al., 2020b), along with differential VOC production upon illumination during confrontation assays.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: High amounts of 2-heptanone are produced during the confrontation against F. oxysporum in a light-dependent manner that negatively correlates with Trichoderma antagonism.
source: High amounts of 2-heptanone are produced during the confrontation against F. oxysporum in a light-dependent manner that negatively correlates with Trichoderma antagonism, which proposes that 2-heptanone production was a result of a stress response elicited by F. oxysporum in the light.
evidence: This statement is supported by the preceding citations to published literature.

claim: Differential interactions in the context of B. cinerea and A. thaliana have been observed, where fungal virulence was enhanced at dusk.
source: We have previously observed differential interactions in the context of B. cinerea and A. thaliana, where fungal virulence was enhanced at dusk (Hevia et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When A. thaliana was infected with Δbcwcl1, it did not show circadian behavior.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed by Hevia et al., 2015, when A. thaliana was infected with Δbcwcl1, which did not show circadian behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The differential outcome of mycoparasitic interactions depending on the time at which confrontations are established could impact biocontrol strategies in agriculture.
source: In nature, organisms are usually exposed to light/dark transitions. Therefore, the differential outcome depending on the time (or the light/dark cycles) at which confrontations are established could impact biocontrol strategies in agriculture, optimizing the application of Trichoderma in crops.
evidence: This is an inference about potential practical applications based on the experimental findings.
